utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brkic. The Chamber takes this opportunity to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made on Wednesday when you declared that you would tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Yesterday we ended a little earlier, and given the situation the witness was in, I suggested that we tender into evidence the Official Note compiled in the police administration of Sisak on the 1st of April, and I would be grateful if this document could be admitted into evidence. 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was extensively discussed yesterday, and it's an Official Note which was not signed by the witness. He only agreed that he testified, but he couldn't -- he cannot say whether it is really his -- we cannot prove that it is really his testimony. It was summarised by a person who signed it, the document, not -- it is not the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Official Note. Are we talking about the Official Note?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about that Official Note from 1992, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest that the Official Note compiled in the police administration in April 1992 and was translated into English by the Prosecution - it also has a B/C/S version - I suggest that this be tendered into evidence. Naturally, the Trial Chamber will decide on the sort of weight that should be attached to this document, and I'd also like to point out that the number on this document is R0184396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you have anything to say on that Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I already stated that I object to tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Exhibit number is 00290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that dispose of the matter of yesterday's witness? My question was are we done with matters relating to the witness who testified yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I have a few questions for re-examination, which we didn't -- we didn't -- we weren't able to start it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you're going to re-examine this witness and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well then. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, yesterday on cross-examination you testified that Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjunovic would receive orders from Knin. It's page 64 of your testimony from yesterday, when Defence counsel asked you about the differences in your statement, and you stated that you do not remember that Martic would -- you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your opposite member is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection I would like to raise, Your Honour. The witness was only answering the questions put to him by the Defence as to whether the statements shown to him and that were provided to the Prosecution stated what has been quoted. Defence counsel's questions were quite different. The witness didn't testify about this matter in response to Defence counsel's questions, and if a question is phrased in this manner, the sense of Defence counsel's initial question is being distorted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to cite exactly what -- what he said yesterday, and I just seek clarification to his answer from yesterday. The witness said: "I don't remember having said that Radjunovic and Kovacevic would go to Knin, but I don't remember that Kovacevic and Radjunovic went to receive orders, but they would receive orders from Knin, from Martic." This is what he said yesterday to Defence counsel's question, and I am just now going to ask a question how -- or how he learned that they -- these two men received orders from -- from Martic. It's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There's nothing I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objection is overruled. You may proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, you testified yesterday that Kovacevic and Radjunovic received orders from Knin, from Martic. Can you tell us, how do you know that they received orders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this from the Serbs when they spoke to each other, from the Serbs who were guarding us, who were with us. This is what we heard when they discussed matters among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Another question is to your answer which we can read on the page 65, when Kovacevic and Radjunovic were relieved of their duties. Do you know whether either of these men were ever investigated or prosecuted after they were relieved of their duties?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also stated that there was -- they -- that they returned. Did they return back to their duties? Was there a time when they returned to their duties?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. After they had been replaced by the JNA and the military police. A few days had gone by, and they then returned to their posts, to their previous positions. They had the authority that they had before, and they enforced the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My last question relates what you testified on page 56. The Defence counsel asked you about the night when the bridge was destroyed and whether -- does that date mean anything to you, and you replied that the day the bridge was destroyed, that shells were hitting houses, the road, the church. Can you explain little bit more what -- what happened? Who did the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling came from the Bosnian side, on the other side of the River Una. It was the Serbs who were shelling the area; the army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also said that cannons were firing at the church. Do you know what happened to this church?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was hit. The tower was hit several times, and a tank opened fire on the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you see it at the time when the -- the shelling took place, or did you see just the result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the result of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was it, approximately, when you saw what happened to the church?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps on the 16th or 17th. Since I was imprisoned on the 15th, on the 16th and 17th we had already started doing our work, and that's when I saw what had happened to the church and to the other houses and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Witness. I'm sorry to have to take you back to these events with the two dead bodies of Antun Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza. May I ask you the following questions for clarification: You named persons who, as you said, were present when you were ordered to load these two bodies on a truck. This is page 3318, line 4. You were asked who were they, and then you said: "I mean the Serbs, because there was Stevo Radjunovic, Momcilo Kovacevic, Mirko Sarac, Milan Petrovic, Djordje Ratkovic, Djuro Jerinic, Marjan Prvalo, all Serbs." Then you added a name, Mladen Pozar. Now, my question is do you remember who of these ordered you to load the two dead bodies on the truck? This would be my first question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the names is incorrect. The last name, Mladen Pozar. It's not Mladen, it's Misa Pozar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And who of them ordered you this? Who spoke to you before the bodies were loaded on the truck?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevo Ratkovic and Momcilo Kovacevic. Mirko Sarac was also present, as well as Milan Petrovic and the others whom I have already named.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Now you said Stevo Ratkovic, but in the minutes that we have is Stevo Radjunovic and Djordje Ratkovic. Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Stevo Radjunovic or Djordje Ratkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I had Stevo Radjunovic in mind. It was a slip of the tongue again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And now who took these bodies then really on the truck? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't really remember that. I couldn't say who loaded the bodies onto the truck. I know that they did that, Sarac, Petrovic, Radjunovic, and the others. That's what I mean when I say I know that these people loaded them onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Then when you arrived at that bridge, you stated yesterday: "I was ordered to throw them off the bridge, but we were so exhausted that we were not able to lift the bodies. So these Serbs, including Mirko Sarac and Milan Petrovic, and all the others, they took the bodies and threw them." So, again, who first told you to take them from the truck, and who took these bodies then from the truck? Do you maybe remember in detail?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at the bridge, Sarac Mirko and Milan Petrovic were there. And they are the people who carried out the act then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Who then ordered you to go to the other side of the bridge's fence in order to kill you and was stopped then by a patrol? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarac and Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly that you were two persons who were supposed to step on the other side of this fence; and if so, who was the other one?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The other person was Mico Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Mr. Josipovic, I'd like to ask you questions continuing, concerning Antun and Zeljko. I'd like to find out from you when is the last time that you saw the two of them alive, and who were they with and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw them alive was that night when we were beaten. I don't know what the time was. It was perhaps around 3.00 or half past three. That was the last time I saw them alive. When I fell into a coma, when I lost consciousness, I then came to my senses, I heard Mico Coric crying out that they were going to kill them when they took us out again. They poured water over us, and they then ordered us to load these bodies onto a tractor trailer. It was about 3.00 or half past three, I think. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you received a number of beatings. Did you receive injuries as a result of these beatings? Please tell us about the injuries, and if you're able to, show us the injuries.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received injuries. My jaw was broken, dislocated. Then they hit me on the head with an axe, so you can see the scar here. We couldn't shave. We couldn't change our clothes. There was some doctor there, I can't remember what his name was, but he claimed to be some sort of a doctor, and he treated us, warmed our kidneys up, et cetera. And he had some sort of a machete to cut the hedges with. On that occasion, since we told him we didn't even have the time to shave or the possibility of shaving and our beards had grown very long, he said that Ustashas didn't wear beards and that he would shave us with that machete. And on that occasion he cut me under the neck, and then our skin was peeled off with a military boot, with the hard part of a military boot. That's what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: How did your jaw come to be broken?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat us. And I don't know how this happened. I was kicked in the side, or from the side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Who was doing the kicking and the beating at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarac, Petrovic, Ratkovic, Jerinic, all the others I have already mentioned, and there are others whose names I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This is a very simple question, but for my own education, Mr. Josipovic, what is a howitzer? Please explain to me.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A howitzer. Well, it's a -- it's a sort of cannon. It has a fairly long range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I am very grateful to you. Thank you. You mentioned in your evidence a captain who went to see Mico Coric or his mother. Now, the record says captain first class. What was the name of that captain, for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you the name, but could I avoid mentioning the name, because I'd like to avoid problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can go into private session if -- so it wouldn't be displayed publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. May the Chamber go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we satisfied that that protective measure will satisfy the witness's requirements?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be erased from public documents, but of course the witness still can refuse to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we will find out when we are in private session. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You mentioned towards the early part of your evidence Serb renegades, and you said that they were waiting and weapons were unloaded from a helicopter and put into trucks and other passenger vehicles that had been seized earlier. From whom were they seized, under what circumstances, and when? Are you able to say? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those vehicles belonged to the former Electra company. They were the property of Electra and of the Croatian forestry company. And there were some other privately owned vehicles. I'm not sure who they belonged to, who they were seized from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: How did they come to be seized? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, they worked at the time in such companies. They had such jobs, and they just helped themselves to those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you say "they," who?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally I'm referring to these rebellious Serbs, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And this is the last question: You had mentioned the Ugljevik in Bosnia, and you mentioned that you saw special police units, and you mentioned the word "blue." What significance does that term "blue" have there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that means. I don't know what its meaning is, but while I was working on the bridge, while I was repairing the bridge, I saw such insignia on both sides. They'd go from Bosnia to Croatia, and then they would return from Croatia into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Josipovic. I've got just a few questions. In your statement of 2000, you related an incident when you asked for permission to go to your home from Mateljak, and he refused and somebody gave you permission to go, and in that paragraph you said that your mother was very scared when you got to her home and the villagers told you that they saw JNA helicopters landing close by. And then you said: "JNA was written on the helicopter. A lot of weapons were unloaded from the helicopter and loaded into a civilian truck from the Electra company. Villagers also saw that the truck transported the weapons to the neighbouring Serb villages of Zivaja and Sas." My question to you is: When you say a lot of weapons were unloaded from the helicopter and loaded into a civilian truck, are you telling us something that you saw with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is a jerrycan? I'm sorry, I don't know this thing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a can in which fuel is kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And again in your statement of 2000, just out of an abundance of caution, at page 1, for instance, there is a reference in the sixth paragraph to HDZ party, and further down there is a reference to HZD party. Are those one and the same thing or two different parties?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It must be a typing error; it's one and the same party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'm sorry to have to take you back to some of the questions that were asked by Judge Nosworthy on my right. You referred in your evidence to a number of insignia. You talked of White Eagles, and you talked of Ugljevik special police units blue, worn by men from Bosnia to help by taking their part. What I want to ask from you is: Are you able to tell us what each of these insignia signified? Which unit it belonged to, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know what the insignia meant, but I did see them, I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say at that time you did not know. Do you now know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, perhaps, yes, I might know something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to share your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear you. Can you say that again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me as if they were White Eagles. There were two eagles. As far as I know, White Eagles -- the White Eagles were a kind of Special Purpose Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also -- one of the writings that you referred to was indeed "Special Police Units." Not "Purpose," but Special Police Units. Is there a difference or -- yes, is there a difference between Special Police Units and Special Purpose Units?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's just what I think. It's one and the same, in essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So -- do I understand you to be saying the White Eagles were worn -- were badges worn by the Special Purpose Units? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you know whether the Special Purpose Units belonged to the JNA or to a TO or to ZNG, or what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that they did not belong to the ZNG, because the ZNG was on the Croatian side. But who they belonged to, whether it was the JNA or the Chetniks, I don't know. It was difficult for me to distinguish between them and to know who was who. They were all Chetniks, basically. They all called themselves Chetniks regardless of what unit they belonged to and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I believe you would say the same thing about the sign blue and the sign Ugljevik.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I would say the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Josipovic. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one very brief question, Your Honours, in connection with blue Ugljevik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the witness know that Ugljevik is a place between Bijeljina and Tuzla, and this is quite far away from Hrvatska Dubica? Does the witness know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know where Plavi Ugljevik is at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Josipovic, thank you so much for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you call the next witness, may we just sort of agree what times we're going to stay in court now that we started a little late. I would propose that we sit until half past eleven, take a break to 12.00, sit from 12.00 to quarter to two. I was advised that that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was always under the impression that the maximum of the tapes is an hour and a half, but if the Court has been advised otherwise and we can do that, that's fine with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. I was always under the impression that the maximum the tape can take was one hour 15 minutes, that's why we sit one hour 15 minutes, but I was advised by the court official here that we can sit for one hour, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine with the Prosecution, then, that schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine with us too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. And thank you very much. May we call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Luka Brkic should come back to start his cross-examination. His direct examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before he's called, at what stage are we at? Is he being cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I had just completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remind you, Mr. Brkic, that on Wednesday you made a declaration that you would tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are still bound by that declaration even today to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm Defence counsel for Milan Martic. I will put some questions to you. This stage of your testimony is called the cross-examination. Please make a pause between my question and your answer so that the interpretation service can do its job.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor when you testified here the day before yesterday, you stated that the village guards in Skabrnja were established in June 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the precise date. I never did give you a precise date, but, yes, that was the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that fighting in Skabrnja broke out on the 18th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please wait until I finish my question before you begin answering so that we don't overlap. That's for the interpretation. Thank you. When answering you to the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you received uniforms in Skabrnja about a month before the conflict that broke out on the 18th of November, 1991. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I received it some three, four, or five days before the conflict at the most. The others got them a bit sooner, but it was all around that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing the uniforms you received, you said that they originated from eastern Germany; that you had boots, a helmet, a uniform, and shoulder straps.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that with respect to the shoulder straps there's an error in the transcript. Will you please tell me whether these shoulder straps were part of a uniform that had a belt, a white belt, and two belts over the shoulders?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Wide, not white.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When answering the Prosecutor's questions, you said there were 245 men under arms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never put forward that number. There were three shifts, three times seven is 21. Twenty-one people working in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I may have been referring to another witness, excuse me. Please tell me this: Are you aware of what number of armed men there were in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that. I only knew about the three shifts, the Ambar. We changed shifts until the 18th. As for the numbers of other units, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you received uniforms; I assume a jacket, trousers, boots, a helmet, shoulder straps. Do you know who gave you this equipment and where it came from?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were just rumours going around. It was a Termos [phoen] Uniform from the Eastern Bloc. When that army was dissolved - it used to be the army of East Germany - they probably got rid of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that together with the uniform you got -- you were issued with a Kalashnikov, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think three or four days before the conflict. Probably three days rather than four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Marko Miljanic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was and what his post was, what his duty was in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Miljanic was a soldier in the former army. I think he was a warrant officer. He left the former army, JNA, and became the commander of the Skabrnja Independent Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When he testified before this court as a witness, Marko Miljanic said that he held this duty which you mentioned, commander of the Skabrnja Independent Battalion, and that in this capacity he organised the defence of Skabrnja, Nadin, Zemunik Gornji, Prkos, Zemunik Donji, Galovac, Gorica, and Glavica, and he explained that this was about one-third of Zadar municipality. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, as commander of the Skabrnja Battalion, spoke in his statement about the fact that the unit in Skabrnja was divided into two parts. One was led by Tasef Kardun [phoen], a car mechanic, and the other by Milos Kara [phoen], an electrician. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Miljanic also said that he had been in contact with Petar Sale, the chief of the Crisis Staff of Zadar municipality, and with Ivica Brzoja, the chief of the Zadar MUP, and they coordinated their activities. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Miljanic, as the commander of the Skabrnja Battalion, the commander of the Skabrnja Independent Battalion, explained that on 18th of November, 1991, Mr. Glavic was the duty officer of the battalion. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know who was at that duty and whether anyone was. All I know is about the guard that was called Ambar. That's all I know about on that day. I don't know about anything else on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement - or, rather, in his statement which he gave to the Prosecution, Mr. Miljanic stated that on the 18th of November, 1991, early in the morning on that day when the conflict broke out in Skabrnja, Mr. Glavic was the duty officer of the battalion, and he told him that 50 per cent of the men were resting in a stacionar.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that term means. There was a place near Glavica. Whether that was it, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Skabrnja is on the road between Zadar and Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Zadar-Benkovac road passes by Skabrnja. It doesn't go through Skabrnja, but there's a road branching off the main road leading into Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic told us that there were 14 JNA barracks in Zadar, including Zemunik airport. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know all about that, because I was a reserve soldier. So I know about Sepurine and all the other barracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor the day before yesterday, or your testimony, you said that after you were captured by the JNA in Skabrnja, you were taken by truck to the Benkovac barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these 14 barracks in Zadar, there were also a JNA barracks in Benkovci?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Benkovac, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, on the 20th and 22nd of September, 2000, in the B/C/S version, it's page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Just if the witness could be provided a copy. If he's going to be directed to particular passages, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the Bench can also be advised where to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, we will provide you with the statement a little later. We've started our cross-examination before the break and I didn't expect that. I won't show the witness any material until we provide you with these copies. My colleague from the Defence could go and fetch some copies of that statement or we could do this after the break, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you then delay your questions from that statement until you've got those statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I'll make sure that I do not ask the witness any questions that would make it necessary for him to refer to this particular statement. The questions I'll put to him will be of a general kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct to say that around summer 1991 you set up village guards in Skabrnja and you had a number of checkpoints there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were checkpoints there. There was one at the entrance. That's the one that the three -- that our three groups manned, and those groups came from that part, from the hamlet of Ambar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was this checkpoint formed of?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of a couple of men -- of several men. Passers-by would stop. If you like, I can tell you what happened there. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever let inhabitants pass through that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The troops used it too when they didn't want to use Martic's road. When things turned ugly, the troops passed through. They probably wanted to act in a provocative way to ensure that an attack was launched as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to those checkpoints in Skabrnja, were there any barricades erected on the main road?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a barricade on the main road, but in fact there were three obstacles, three hedgehogs. They weren't obstructing the movement of vehicles; they were by the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say metal hedgehogs.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were made of rail tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose of these obstructions were?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to slow down the traffic, if necessary. If it wasn't necessary, the troops would obtain fuel from the air base and as no one obstructed them, they used the road just like all the other normal citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an air base.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have the Zemunica air base in mind?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Zemunik air base in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how far that air base was from Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Srednja Porta, as said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecutor and in your statements, you also mentioned the shelling of Skabrnja. You mentioned Napalm bombs and cassette bombs.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there was someone called Sinisa and some sort of a girl. They must have been in love but they wrote something down on a shell -- on the shell of a cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did these cluster bombs fall in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right of the church, in front of the church, in the field. That's where these cluster bombs fell.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness didn't say cassette bomb, he said cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said those cluster bombs fell by the church itself. There are two churches in Skabrnja, though.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the main church, St. Mary's, at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, the cluster bomb fell by the main church in the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It started -- they started falling in front of the church. I saw that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was killed by the cluster bombs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one at the time, because the houses weren't affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that church in the centre and the houses that were in the vicinity of the church, how far from the houses did that bomb fall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it fell near the houses or one house that was near the church, but that's where certain parts of the cluster bombs fell, and all the other parts fell in front of the church, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any combat positions there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any combat positions there. Perhaps they thought that there were some mortars located there, but that wasn't the case. Perhaps that's why these bombs were launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In what area, what sort of area was this cluster bomb used?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in an area of about a hundred or 200 metres. That was the area it was used in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And no one was hurt?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned mortars.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received automatic rifles in addition to helmets and uniforms. Was there any -- was there any other weapons apart from the mortars in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were only those mortars. They disappeared on that day. They went to Donje Rastane. They were taken to Donje Rastane. They were there before, but on that day in the evening they disappeared. I myself don't know where they were taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many mortars were there? Who used them and who took them away?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you who the crews were. There were two, three -- there were three mortars. And there was ZIS that didn't have its shell. It was by the church of St. Mary's, the second, smaller church in Ambar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is a ZIS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a one-barrelled weapon that is used to attack a tank or a moving vehicle, anything of that kind. It is used instead of a hand-held launcher. It's a recoilless cannon, one could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were on guard the night before the attack.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were on a shift. You were replaced by another shift that consisted of seven or eight men.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you returned from the checkpoint, you went to your brother's house, you took off your uniform, and you had civilian clothes on under your uniform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you left your guard post, did you take your automatic rifle with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These men who replaced you at the guard post or at the checkpoint in the morning when the conflict broke out, were they also wearing uniforms, and did they have automatic rifles too?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They probably had uniforms, because they replaced me at 3.00 -- early in the morning; 3.00 precisely. So they were probably wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When fire was opened in Skabrnja, you said that you were in your brother's house, you were sleeping, you heard some sort of a shell that fell behind the house. You then went out to see what was happening. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that a JNA unit arrived in Skabrnja that morning? It stopped in front of the entrance to the village by the hamlet of Ambar, and the officer heading the unit got out of a tank with the intention of speaking to those present, and in order to ensure that the population who were armed surrender. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps subsequently hear that this officer was -- had the surname Stefanovic, after he had got out of the tank to negotiate about finding a peaceful solution to the situation in Skabrnja, he was killed? Another soldier stepped in to help him when he fell, and that soldier was also killed on that occasion. It's only then that an all-out armed conflict broke out. Do you know anything about this, about the second lieutenant who was killed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you were taken to the barracks in the Benkovac after having been imprisoned -- after having been arrested, you said you were driven there by a JNA soldier who was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that we were taken there in a bus. This person was probably from Rastevic but it's not necessarily so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, do you remember having said that this JNA soldier who was in a unit that had arrived in Skabrnja said that he didn't know or that the soldiers didn't know that an attack would be launched?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me when I was returning. He said he was going to Benkovac after Skabrnja had fallen, after everything that happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you heard the shooting, you said that you crawled out of the house, you saw that fire was being opened from machine-guns, and you saw tanks.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I saw some going over a field. I saw this with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point in time you climbed onto the roof of the house to have a better view of the situation, and at the time some sort of a mortar shell fell on the roof.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was a small mortar shell. It broke some sort of a window. It fell in front of the house. Later, I saw the case of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you said that you had a helmet at the time.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I went out, I had a helmet on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you observe the situation from the roof? Did you have to move the tiles?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's a big balcony door. There's a sloping roof. I opened the balcony door. There's a small wall in front of you. I saw a few men down below. I then returned back, and that's when the shell hit the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing the tanks that entered the village, you said that they were coming from the direction of the village of Ambar, from the entrance to the village where the first church is located.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the main entrance into the village. There were others approaching from Polje. There were three of them. Two were going to Sveta Luka. A third one wanted to head directly towards my house but it got stuck in the mud. And there was another one coming from a field called Dunjevac. That reached the transformer station and joined the first tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said that when you saw these tanks and since they were coming from the direction of the hamlet of Ambar, which is at the very beginning of the village, you said that some individuals were killed in that first attack, some individuals who were manning the checkpoint and who had replaced you. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they opened fire on JNA troops that were arriving in the village that morning?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There was intensive shooting. At the time certain facilities were on fire. It was terrible. There was a lot of screaming, a lot of noise. You couldn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is how you describe all the noise and all the chaos, that you said that you heard some people shouting out, "Get hold of him."

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. It wasn't that far away. It was about a hundred metres or 130 metres away. So it was possible for people to speak to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you came down from the roof and those men at the first checkpoint withdrew to where you were located.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the second group that came to see me and see what they should do. That's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Did you tell those people that they should go to the road where it would be easier to defend the village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I warned them because the tank was about 30 metres away. It was barely possible to cross the road without being killed. They then left. I told them to flee from the village. I said if you're at risk, there's nothing you can do. It will all be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you tell them to go to the centre of the village, wasn't it dangerous in the centre of the village too?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These men from Rasovljeva and Glava hadn't yet arrived. These were tanks that were going through Marinovac Cesta. There was a second entrance there, another entrance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you then went to your brother's house to see what sort of situation the people in the cellar were in. You mentioned 16 or 17 men.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were neighbours, the neighbours' children, there were three neighbours there, there were small babies, children who were about 8 or 9 or 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, there's a sentence that says: "The attack resumed at around 11.00." Do you remember that brief sentence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a brief lull of 15 to 20 minutes. It was difficult to measure the time. One didn't look at one's watch to see when it started and when it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that when you got down from the attic where you were observing the situation, you went down into the basement and you saw those people there. Among them were the people whose last name was Burlica [as interpreted]. You also said there was a light machine-gun, two automatic rifles, an automatic rifle, and as you said, a shotgun in the basement.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was carrying these weapons? Who had brought them there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shotgun, that's a hunting rifle, was already there. The Kalashnikov was mine, I had brought it there. The light machine-gun -- the submachine-gun belonged to Neno Gurlica who had -- to whom it had been issued before that. Pero Gurlica had a weapon we referred to as the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I recall you explained to the Prosecutor in the course of your testimony that you counselled the people who were in the basement, Marijan, Neno, and Petar Gurlica to change clothes.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. I did have some life experience, and I assumed something bad might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the following: At that point in time, you were a mature man. You were armed. Those three were also armed with serious artillery weapons. When the JNA came along amid this general shooting, you fled into the basement among the women and children. Did you do this because you were afraid or because you thought the JNA would not harm women and children?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them not to open fire. The tanks were close, and you couldn't do anything to attack. Someone could get killed on the other side, but we didn't dare shoot because the people in the basement might have got killed. We didn't want to shoot because we wanted the others to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the advent of the tanks. Do you remember that two or three days before the conflict in Skabrnja broke out a Special Purpose Unit commanded by Djuro Zupan arrived in Skabrnja? There were 20 or 30 men armed with special anti-tank rockets, and their task was to destroy the tank grouping in Veljun. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a small group of young men from Skabrnja for the most part but they didn't have weapons. You could have parked your tanks there and nothing would have happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went down into the basement among the women, children, and the other people there, that there was some 18 to 20 of you, and that the soldiers came up to the house, banged on the door and demanded that you open up.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They broke down the balcony door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you whether you had weapons and did they find weapons in the basement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: When they were banging of the door, little Neno had not yet managed to take off his boots. The other man had a tracksuit on, he spent the whole winter in it, and that's how it came about that he had to sleep in it, although it was cold. I went out and I told them there were civilians inside. I asked them not to throw a hand grenade in. They were threatening to do that, but they didn't. They ordered me to get the ladder and pull it up so that he could go down if he wanted to. They changed their mind about throwing the hand grenade in and then the women and children started getting out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that thanks to this situation the submachine-gun, the two automatic rifles and the shotgun were not found?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they should put the weapons in a visible place, and they were able to see them. That's as far as the submachine-gun goes. The other rifles remained hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the army saw those weapons and when you got outside, you explained that they ordered you men to lie down, and I assume they searched you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did search us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained here in the course of your testimony that after that the soldiers separated off the women and children and sent them towards the edge of the village and that you and the Gurlicas were taken along with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Describing your movements together with the soldiers, you provided a detail and I'll remind you of it. You said a tank went in front. This Captain Jankovic was going right next to the caterpillar tracks, so he was taking shelter behind the tank.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were right next to the captain, with your hands up in the air, and the Gurlicas were behind you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also described, as far as I was able to understand you, that there were one or two tanks behind you. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other tanks as well, and there was a combat armoured vehicle, a BOV, which had an anti-aircraft machine-gun, a PAM, on it. And there was also an armoured vehicle where ammunition is transported on caterpillar tracks. It's used to transport ammunition. And all this was right next to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that your capture, your exit from the basement, the separating off of the men from the women and children, and your departure towards the church with Captain Jankovic, that all this took place around noon.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it went on until first dusk, around 6.00. You couldn't look around. I couldn't even put my hands down. It was only at around 6.00 p.m. that I asked if I could put my hands down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that in this situation, walking alongside the captain who had previously saved you, the four of you were walking behind the tanks, that you approached the church, and at one point somebody fired or, rather, opened fire on the tank.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was three bullets, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that at one point the captain pulled you back and said, "Take shelter. Your own people will kill you."

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time you were with the tanks and with this captain, and you were observing the situation fully.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw more than Captain Jankovic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break I'll put another question. There was a Prosecution witness here, Mr. Miljanic, the commander of the Skabrnja Battalion, and he said that at one point he wanted heroically to hit the tank with a rocket launcher but that the tank was surrounded with women and children and that they were a human shield, whereas you are saying that the women and children were separated off right away and sent towards the hamlet of Ambar at the edge of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have been referring to the other tanks going from Biljane towards Glavica. I saw those as well. I had even been there at Oscar's for three days. There were lots of soldiers there before the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The other member is on his feet, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just wonder if I could have a reference because we're trying as best we can to follow along in Mr. Miljanic's testimony, but what I see are references civilians, not women and children. So I would like to have a reference, what Defence counsel is referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 2876, line 10, the testimony of Witness Miljanic, Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that 2876 page, line 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, and we can sort out those --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break, come back at 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we will continue your cross-examination now. Let me remind both of us once again that we should make a pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpretation. When describing the arrival of the soldiers in your brother's house where you were in the basement, you said that you heard the soldiers breaking down the door outside on the terrace, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With reference to the question put to you as to the ethnic affiliation of the soldiers, you explained they were regular soldiers, conscripts serving their military service. You even mentioned a lad from Zagreb, whereas in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, on page 4 in B/C/S, the fifth passage from the top, you say that among the soldiers breaking into your house you heard some speaking Albanian. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the one who was speaking Albanian was down on the road. A lot of things in the statement are not in the place where they should be but a bit before or after. So it should be fixed a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could one say that in that JNA unit which was in Skabrnja at the time there were soldiers of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can assume that. Or, rather, you could observe it by the way they spoke. As I said, there was one from Zagreb. He was a conscript doing his military service. And when I ended up in Knin, I heard a lot of others who were similarly serving their army service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described what was going on around the church, and you said that on the 18th of November, 1991, the fighting went on until dusk and that then you went towards Ambar hamlet at the outskirts of the village.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please don't skip over things and then stray off the main topic. It -- shall we talk about not just the real soldiers, the regular soldiers, but all those who were present?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will put those questions to you which I consider important.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have been examined in detail and given a lot of explanations, so I will only ask about those things which in the opinion of Defence should be further explained. You said that in the evening of the 18th you were taken to the JNA barracks in Benkovac. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained in detail how this happened, and I will remind you of a part of your statement where you say -- and that's on page 5, the last passage on page 5 -- you said that on the road you briefly stopped in Biljane where you saw a huge pile of weapons which you believed was confiscated from Skabrnja. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the first statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You speak of a big pile of weapons captured in Skabrnja. What was in that pile? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the classical kind of infantry weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described how after you had spent a night in the barracks in Benkovac, after breakfast you were taken to another barracks, this time in Knin. Was that the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a JNA barracks called Juzni Logor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in the prison premises, which you described in detail, and can you tell us whether you know whether this was a military prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It used to be a military prison. Later on, all the formations that were around were there. I didn't have time to check that. Later on, I learned that there were all sorts of people there; Martic's men and others, and I don't know who stayed there for how long, but I know that there was a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was as follows: You were captured by the JNA, taken by the JNA first to the barracks in Benkovac and from there to the barracks in Knin, and it was they who put you in prison there. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that after a certain time you were taken from the Juzni Logor prison in the barracks to the place where you were to make -- to make railings on windows in Knin hospital.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number of us went there; Blaskic, Sinovcic, some people from Drnis and the surrounding area, a man called Lacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in the old hospital where you were working on the bars of the windows, were there people there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people who were already in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, you explained that you were exchanged in May.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of May precisely.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you described the area where you built bars or for which you built bars, you said that people called it Martic's prison.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they called it. There was some other fortress, but I don't know whether that's the prison or some other prison, but they called this the old hospital or Martic's prison. I didn't hear any other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Martic in that prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw Mr. Martic there. Perhaps he was standing next to me, but I wouldn't have recognised him, I wouldn't have known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you said that you saw Mladic in the prison in Knin on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you described your second meeting with him or second time you saw him, you said that was at the beginning of March 1992, and Mladic was there with the chief of staff, Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of them, but they told me that this person was Vukovic, but I didn't know those officers. I had never seen those officers before. They arrived by helicopter. They were wearing leather clothes, leather jackets. I remember that Mladic had a cherry coloured torch that he would play with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion Mladic was there with Vukovic, the officer Vukovic and other officers. They were inspecting the situation, and they were involved in the exchange of prisoners, but after Vukovic arrived things proceeded more easily. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you knew the officer Mladic, but according to all the information that is available, according to all the evidence, all the information that Defence has, Vukovic was the commander of the 9th Corps up until 1992, and Colonel Mladic was his chief of staff, but you are saying that in March 1992, the chief of staff was involved in an inspection with the general. Have you confused something?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He even came to boast in front of us. He asked us, "Do you know who we are?" "I'm General Mladic." He came to boast in front of us. So when he arrived there, he already held the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that he came with his chief of staff, Officer Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told. I didn't know Mr. Vukovic. A certain man called Bracic knew all the officers in Knin and he told me that this person was Vukovic. He also pointed out some other individuals to me, but I haven't thought about this for a long time, so I don't remember the names very well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to weapons and equipment that the battalion in Skabrnja had, the battalion that was under the command of Miljanic, there is information according to which, during two days of combat in Skabrnja, on the first day two soldiers were killed whereas five were wounded, and on the second day two other soldiers were killed and five were wounded, and JNA soldiers are being referred to. There is even written evidence that on that occasion in Skabrnja a total of 14 mortars were captured, the calibre of which was between 60 and 120 millimetres. On one day seven mortars were captured and on the second day another seven. 50 automatic rifles were captured, 37 hand grenades were captured, a recoilless cannon was seized, seven cases of ammunition the calibre of which was 7.62 were seized. That would be ammunition for an automatic rifle. Do you know anything about this quantity of weapons seized in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the mortars are concerned, the figure is not correct. If there were any mortars, there were no more than six or seven mortars, if there were any at all. Everything else is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that there were three of them; the commander of the defence says that there were two.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it's possible that there were seven of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please let me finish my question and then you will tell me what you know. I'm not objecting to you, I'm just putting a question to you. Mr. Miljanic gave evidence under oath and said that the men had no uniforms, that they had nothing, that there were only two small mortars, and you are now saying that there were perhaps six mortars. You said that there were uniforms, helmets, belt supports, rifles. You're saying that there was a Skabrnja battalion in existence. Whose battalion was this?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was said at the very beginning; the Independent Skabrnja Battalion. Marko Miljanic must have told you about its strength. And then the mortars that have been referred to were taken to Donje Rastane, and then from Donje Rastane they were taken to Crvena Luka, so on that day even if there were two mortars, that was too many. So Marko Miljanic was perhaps quite right in saying that there were two mortars there, but I don't know about those two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could I just have a reference to that portion of Miljanic's testimony, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to point out to my learned colleague that this is the statement -- the written statement that the Witness Miljanic gave to the Prosecution, and it also concerns his evidence at this trial. The page is 2873. This concerns Miljanic's evidence before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Miljanic also mentioned a minefield that had been laid in the vicinity of the airport. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The airport?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Dusevna hospital.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. He later participated in this or was part of the engineer system. It was mined and that was done well. The land strip was blown up and I think that a French person died on that occasion. And that was quite late.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The building mentioned was a mental hospital, not Dusevna hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Another question concerns a written document in which a colonel describes what he -- in which a lieutenant describes what he found in the field in Skabrnja after the action in Skabrnja. He mentions everything he found in Skabrnja, including sites where dead men and women were found, whether in uniform or in civilian clothes, and he mentions -- and he drew a sort of diagram, a sketch of Skabrnja. He mentions the fact that in the centre of Skabrnja there was a large garage with the inscription The Andrija Artukovic Weaponry Barracks. There were weapons there, ammunition, hand grenades. Do you know anything about the Andrija Artukovic barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I think that this has been manipulated. I doubt that anyone had a radio set of any kind at the time. Perhaps somebody had a walkie-talkie but, I doubt that too. But that's possible. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question for you. As a man who in the late spring and then summer and autumn, as a man who was in Croatia at the time, did you hear anything about the JNA barracks being blocked in Croatia,? For example, in Split, in Sibenik, in Sinj, in Zadar, in Karlovac, and before that in Gospic, in Zagreb, in Varazdin, in Bjelovar, in Osijek, Sisak, Slavonski Brod, Virovitica, later on in Vukovar? Have you heard anything about these JNA barracks being under a blockade?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entire public knew something about that, so why would I have to think about this in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witnesses who have appeared before this Chamber have also testified that in Kijevo there were some Croatian armed forces. We've heard this from you, that they were present in Drezni Grad, in Rakovica, in Slunj, in Bacin, in Cerovljani, in Dubica, but the headquarters under Mateljak's command was located in Hrvatska Dubica. I have now mentioned a series of villages that Marko Miljanic mentioned they were under his command. Do you know of any other places where there were armed men?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness. Counsel for the Prosecution is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for the interruption again. I'd like to have a cite for that, please, because I think it misstates the evidence. I don't remember Mr. Miljanic saying that he was in control in Slunj and Bacin and Dubica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, Your Honour. Mr. Miljanic didn't say that, nor did I. I was only quoting the testimony of other witnesses who spoke about the situation in other villages, and at the end I said that Mr. Miljanic spoke not only about Skabrnja but about another six or seven villages in the municipality of Zadar. So I was very precise. I don't know whether my learned colleague was following me well and whether my words were correctly interpreted. My question was as follows: In the course of evidence given by various witnesses here, we have heard that there were Croatian armed forces in Kijevo. The witness said that they were also present in Skabrnja. Other witnesses said that they were present in Saborsko, Drezni Grad, Rakovica, Slunj.
