Other witnesses, for example, the witness who was here today, mentioned Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani and the headquarters or the command, the main staff in Hrvatska Dubica, and Mateljak was in command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This strikes me as argument, Your Honour. This witness has not testified about any of these places and it's unclear to me what possible comment he could have on the rather lengthy question from counsel. I'd ask that he put questions to the witness rather than argue to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That sounds like a legitimate objection, Mr. Milovancevic. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I haven't put my question to the witness yet. My colleague interrupted me. The introduction was rather lengthy, but my question is as follows: Given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't put your question yet. Let's finish with your objection. My problem, and this is a problem of the Chamber, that indeed you put very long sentences before you put your questions. Just look at that line from page 44 from line 15 to line 25. You are saying -- it's just you speaking there. Then you put a question, and that question seems to refer to everything that you have spoken about, and neither -- not the witness nor the Bench nor your opposite number understand what your question relates to. Put questions to this witness, and if his testimony differs with the testimony of other witnesses and you want to put those to him, take them one by one. You've mentioned lots of villages here. Now, the objection is that the witness has not testified about these villages. Just take these one by one, one sentence at a time, one fact at a time. Then we will understand. There will be no confusion. Please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll put a short question to you. I previously asked you whether you had heard about JNA barracks being under blockade. Now you have just told us about what you did in Skabrnja. Do you believe that you participated in an armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is how things were -- Your Honours, may I tell you what the truth was about many things that you are confused about? I could do that in a few words. It would be more rapid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have answered my question. You said that you did not participate in an armed rebellion, and that is enough for me. Thank you. Given everything that took place in Skabrnja in November 1991, you mentioned Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav People's Army. All of this took place in your village, too, and you had helmets, rifles, uniforms, a staff and an organisation. Was all this organised in such a manner so that you could confront the federal army?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People -- they had already started capturing people. Martic's people had already taken an excavator from a relative of mine. I had to take him to Crvena Luka, which was full of police. They were eating and drinking, I don't know what they were doing. I took the excavator away without asking them for permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question for you and that will then conclude my cross-examination. Are you aware of the fact that the headquarters for Central and Northern Dalmatia, with its base in Zadar, signed an agreement with the JNA at the beginning of October 1991 on raising the blockade of all the barracks that had been placed under a blockade in the area? Do you know anything about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Defence counsel has no further questions for this witness. This concludes our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No problem at all, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I just have a couple more questions for you. First, you remember that as my colleague the Defence lawyer was putting questions to you, he asked you about some JNA soldiers coming to the entrance to Skabrnja, to Ambar, and asking the villagers whether they wanted to surrender. Do you remember those questions that the Defence lawyer asked you about?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll see if I can help you remember. The question was: "Are you aware of the fact that a JNA unit arrived in Skabrnja that morning? It stopped in front of the entrance to the village by the hamlet of Ambar, and the officer heading the unit got out of a tank with the intention of speaking to those present and in order to ensure that the population who were armed surrendered. Are you aware of that fact?" And you said, "No, I'm not." Do you remember that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes. Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that. How far away from the entrance to Ambar were you there when you were staying at your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 130, 140 metres, ten metres more or less. It's not far. It's the fifth house if you count the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you hear any gunfire that morning before you heard the first shells falling?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I heard that first shell, then there was intensive shooting. First they started targeting the church and the centre, and it was the PAM that fired the most shots, and then all the weapons started firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did that appear to you to be a spontaneous attack or something that had been planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was planned in advance. There had been barricades set up already. We've skipped over a lot of things here. I explained it to you when we talked. A lot of things have remained unsaid. Everybody knows from Sibenik onwards their forces had set up barricades, and it was only then that we responded to protect our village, to stop them passing through and provoking and so that we would know what was happening in the village. That was the reason for the barricades, not to attack. It was pure defence, defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why do you think Skabrnja was attacked?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one reason, which transpired later on; the Virovitica-Karlobag corridor. That was their intention ever since the Austrian war long ago. It was nothing spontaneous. It was something they have wanted for a very long time. It's very simple. It doesn't take long to explain it. Of course they were looking for an excuse. First Martic's road was built, which the people will always remember, going from the airport through the Orthodox village of Smokovic, Gornje Biljane, Biljane, Smicic [phoen], Benkovac. That was their route which they had in case they couldn't use the Zadar-Benkovac road. I went to take a car to my daughter in Plitvice, her new Skoda, and in Plitvice they had already put two tank barrels together. I travelled on that road. I went through Obrovac, the so-called Glinica, and as I was registered as a car -- as a transporter in Knin or Obrovac, I paid the -- I bought them a drink. I gave them some beer. I was afraid they would confiscate my car. And then I went on through Maslica [phoen]. All these stories, that's all in vain. All it was was self-defence, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say "they," it was something they had wanted for a long time, who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the SAO Krajina. It wasn't just Martic. There were others as well, but he was playing his role there. It was all a matter of the Krajina and Greater Serbia, nothing else. And the Posavina corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about a different topic. You were asked on cross-examination about the weapons that were in the cellar when you were in the cellar of your brother's house. Do you remember being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did put questions about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just one further question: Once you and the others came out of the cellar, did you have any weapons with you then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. How could you have weapons when you were already captured? Who would you take them to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question that Defence counsel asked you about, they said, "Could one say that in that JNA unit which was in Skabrnja at the time there were soldiers of all ethnicities?" And then you gave an answer, and then when Defence counsel wanted to move on to something else you said, "Please don't skip over things and stray off the main topic. Shall we talk about not just the real soldiers, the regular soldiers, but all those who were present." And then the Defence lawyer didn't give you a chance to explain, he went on to something else. What did you want to say about all those present, not just the regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that I meant that they were mostly reservists. There were very few regular soldiers. The regular soldiers didn't know what was going on. They were lads who had been somehow misled, and they themselves talked about it later on. By -- I met the same soldier who beat me. He was a Siptar, an Albanian, and he told me that he -- he came to see us and provoke us when he was coming to collect his salary. He said he had wanted to kill us. He was boasting about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about the reservists. Do you think that they knew what was going on in Skabrnja that day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- this re-direct is now referring to matters not raised by the Defence during the cross-examination, and they were dealt with extensively during the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just refer to page 37 of the transcript where this issue is raised. The witness, in response to my first question on this topic, said that he was explaining and he said he meant mostly reservists. He said the regular soldiers didn't know what was going on, which led to my question what about the reservists, what did he think they knew?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my objection was one of principle. The question I put to the witness referred only to the ethnic make-up of the JNA troops. The Defence felt this was a topic that had to be raised. However, now we are moving on to something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When the witness wanted to answer you, you stopped him. That's why the Prosecution wants to know what it is the witness wanted to say to you which you didn't want to hear, because the Prosecution is interested in hearing it. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, perhaps you don't know, and if you don't know, that's fine, but do you know today the ethnicity of any of those reservists that participated in the attack on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were our neighbours from neighbouring villages, Zemunik Gornja, Veljane, Biljane, Gornje Biljane, all those hamlets up to Djevrske and Kistanje. It was a large area: Lisane, Rastevic, all the Orthodox villages, they all participated. We have information on this. There is no need to talk about it a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say "Orthodox," is that the same as saying Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Serb villages. I'm not disparaging that, it's just our way of talking. If they want to declare themselves as Serbs, it's their right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. One further question for you, Mr. Brkic. Defence counsel also asked you about Martic's prison, and he asked you if you'd ever seen Martic there, and you said, "No, I never saw Mr. Martic there. Perhaps he was standing next to me, but I wouldn't have recognised him, I wouldn't have known him." And my question for you is very simply: Did you know at that time what Milan Martic looked like?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, as to this map which the Prosecution presented on Wednesday and of which we got these large bluish copies marked for identification under number 285, the original of which, according to your statement, was found after Operation Storm among a lot of the other documents in a place that housed the police administration at that time.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You stated it shows -- the map shows the course of the attack on Skabrnja and that you assume the attackers drew this map. Now I have two or three questions to that. First, you said you obtained the map from the people who were involved in Operation Storm. Can you give us more specific information when and from whom you obtained the map?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it about two or three months ago. I knew of its existence earlier, but I didn't think I needed it. I described this because everything that's on this map is something I have seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And from whom did you obtain the map?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it from a man who got it from a colleague who probably still works in the police and who had access to those premises. The man who gave it to me is called Gurlica. He's a neighbour of mine. He's a close friend of this man who gave it to him. Who else could have given it to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In which condition was this map when you got it? Was this a copy or the original, and in which condition was that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a copy. The map was in poor condition. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So this could be an explanation for the following question: As the Defence counsel pointed out on Wednesday, the handwritten notes partly are in ball pen, others -- actually, most of the marks and notes in and around the map were written with felt pen. Actually, to me it looks like having been traced what was already written with ball pen for better legibility. This seems obvious to me. Can you explain to us who used the black marker? I suppose this was before the copy was made.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was done before. I see no reason for somebody to write over it without any need. I wouldn't see the purpose of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So you don't know --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- who did the markings, the tracing with that --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the notes were made by the persons who were making this plan. I don't think any other person could have done that or would need to do that. Who else could fabricate or imagine such a plan and write down names they didn't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Those were my questions, just on those technical issues, so this is all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I add one question? Do you know if the original still exists and when -- and if, where and who has it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. If it does exist, I could get it, but I doubt it. It was a crumpled up piece of paper. Somebody smoothed it out and then made a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I do have quite a few questions to ask you, and I want to start off by asking you this: You say that you're from Skabrnja, but what ethnic group are you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question is that you said in your evidence you were called a Siptar, and you explained that this term meant somebody from Kosovo, an Albanian. And you said, or it forms part of the transcript, that you believe this was done to facilitate your liquidation. Should that be to prevent or avoid your liquidation?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Absolutely to avoid your liquidation?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no reason, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I thought on this point you had said originally that the person was trying to save you. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Siptars in that village. I was caught in my own yard. Well, my house and my brother's house shared the same yard. How could there be Siptars or Albanians in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I see what you mean. Now, you said in evidence and you touched on it not so long ago that the soldiers with Captain Jankovic were picked from surrounding villages, but you also said that there were persons with paint on their faces, and you only recognised one who spoke to you in relation to the cord that was for the cleaning of your gun. Now, in view of the fact that they had paint on their faces and you didn't recognise them, how were you able to say that they were from surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This guy was from Gornji Zemunik. We knew them whether they had paint on their faces or not. We had been in contact before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All of --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our private lives, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're saying this relates to all of the persons who had paint on their faces or just the one who you say recognised you because -- who spoke to you concerning the cleaning of the gun with the cord?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had paint on their faces whether they were reservists or regulars. The one from Gornji Zemunik, his nickname was Gusa, he did not have paint on his face. That's how I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. I'm going to ask you now a question: The basement of your brother's house or, rather, that house that you were in, was it significant to the village guard or the duties of the village guard in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was considered to be the safest shelter, the safest basement in that cluster of houses. All the houses had basements, but this basement was the most secure one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you also said on Wednesday that you were taken to Knin where initially you were detained in the south camp. This camp had barracks. Do you know if these barracks had any special or specific name?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called Juzni Logor, which means "south camp." I don't know whether it bore any other name after some national hero. There was another barracks called Slavko Rodic. I know that we'd been there. We had gone to unload barracks, to unload ammunition there from Gornji Rok. That's not anywhere in the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question is that you testified that you were held in the barracks for approximately five months, and you said, They detained us in the barracks until we cleared everything, and you mentioned the arrival of Pajo's helmets. What or who are Pajo's helmets? Please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was UNPROFOR. The first troops arrived and they saw us working and they were angry to see prisoners working, and they chased some of them off, saying they shouldn't work. It was towards the end. Things had already been cleaned up, prepared, concealed, things that they were not supposed to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. And my next question to you is as follows: You testified that the people who remained, as you had already said, they no longer had the five-pointed star, they had the JA insignia, the Yugoslav army insignia, and the Serbian flag, and that was the sort of insignia they had, and you didn't see anything else. The SAO Krajina, well, this is something you could see on all of them. And then there was the JA insignia and the White Eagles, the Beli Orlovi insignia, but I didn't see anything else. As for the individuals who were wearing the cockade hats, et cetera, in Benkovac, well, what's different? Please allow me to finish because I'm going to ask you some questions, Mr. Brkic. If you would just be patient with me. These are my questions: You mentioned Beli Orlovi insignia. Is that for the same unit as the White Eagles or would it be a different unit? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were Captain Dragan's units. They were in the attack on Skabrnja, but they were not in the barracks. They were up there in Golubic, and I don't know where else. But whenever the helicopter landed on the helicopter landing pad, it would always fly off towards that camp, whether it was Mladic or another officer or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: While you were at that position, did you know Captain Dragan's real name?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw the man. I just saw his men. They asked me whether I knew what their insignia meant. I did know, but I didn't dare answer because I was afraid - this was still in Skabrnja - because they participated in all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Was Captain Dragan in charge or command of the White Eagles or was it somebody else, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the only one. Whether there was somebody coordinating this with him, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question on this area: Do you know who was in charge of the unit wearing the cockade caps?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to let me say that. It wasn't units with cockades, it was individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It was individuals? And who was in charge of the unit in which those individuals were who had the cockade caps then? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some in every unit who wore those cockades. Anyone who wanted to would put it on his head and wear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. My next question to you: You mentioned the cockades and World War II. Who used to wear them in World War II?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chetniks. Draza Mihajlovic's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Chetniks meaning who?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Priest Djuic's men. The Chetniks had their "cetas," or companies. "Ceta" means company, so that's why they were called Cetniks, whereas the Ustashas had risen up, and in Croatian you say "ustasi." That's where the word comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do Chetniks have anything to do with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were paramilitary units they had at the time, the period that we are discussing now. But they -- there were very few such men at the time. They weren't very strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you mentioned Captain Jankovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well. I'm glad that I recall him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you said that he was -- you believed that he was Vojvodina. I might not be pronouncing it right.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You pronounced it correctly. They called him Lala, so I assumed he was from there because they call people from Vojvodina Lala, but I don't know whether that was the case. I didn't know this person from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I couldn't translate that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Vojvodina is a Croat or a Serb village or a place?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I put it? It's an independent province. Of a temporary or permanent kind, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question is you said that one soldier told you in respect of reservists, I think, that -- or soldiers, these are the White Eagles, and he said the soldiers belonged to the reservists, and you said you could see it from their faces -- or you said, rather, that the soldiers belong to the reservists and you could see it from their faces. Why did you say you could see it from their faces? Please hold on for me. Did you recognise them or was there something special about their faces or what was on their faces?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were masked or camouflaged, but I saw that these men were not all young men. There were mature men among them. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: How did you reach the conclusion that they were reservists? From their faces you said you could see it. That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the arrival in Benkovac, I saw people whom I personally knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: These were not masked persons?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the church in the village in the centre of Skabrnja. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And I wanted to know about that church. What denomination was it? Was it Orthodox Serb, Croatian, Catholic, Protestant? What was it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Catholic church. The church of St. Mary's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And was it Croat or Serb or ...

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, the persons who beat you will in the lorry or the truck on the way to Knin, how did you know that they were part of the army of soldiers in the barracks at Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two persons called Pupovac, I knew them myself. I'd been in their house. I'd worked with the father. He was involved in transport, like myself. We worked in Lika, Crvena Jezera. We'd transport goods to various destinations. Perhaps it's not necessary to mention all of this, but we often worked together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned people who were brought into the sports hall, who kept on coming, arriving and leaving. Are you able to tell us what ethnic group those persons belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly Croats. As far as I can remember, there were two Serbs, too. One was called Lalic, and there was another person who arrived in Zadar, and unfortunately he hanged himself there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to hear that. Now --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to ask you this question, please: In respect of the detainees in the old hospital, Martic prison, in Martic's prison, were they mainly men or were there any females?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the persons who were being held there, not the personnel.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mainly men. I can only remember one woman who was from the Croatian armed forces, from the HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies. And where specifically was this lady being held, this one woman?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw her by a window in the vicinity of the toilets. That's as you look in that direction from the nursery, it was in the left wing. If you look from the grounds of the hold hospital in the direction of the west, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And this is my last question, you'll be pleased to hear. Did you receive any injuries at all as a result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many injuries. My face was changed. About 70 per cent of my face was modified. I've now returned back to normal, at least to a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What specifically do you mean by your face being modified?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd been poisoned twice. Now you can see sort of protuberances beneath the skin. I had to have surgical interventions. Then I used certain medicine and that helped. I went to see some doctors in Long Beach because I didn't believe the other doctors, but that's how it is; when you are at risk, you are suspicious, you don't trust anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Any other injuries?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my ribs were broken and stretched apart, and I have some scar tissue. You can see where I was hit, where I was beaten. My left leg was swollen. I had to -- I was supposed to go and have my leg X-rayed recently, but because of this hearing, because of the evidence I'm giving here, I couldn't. So all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Any of the injuries to your upper body in a position where you can show the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only in this area where the tissue was ripped apart. When I lie down and get up, it moves in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Brkic, at the time in 1991, did the Yugoslav People's Army have a military base in Ambar?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Skabrnja there was a reserve airport that was used by the American army in the former war. It was then used by the Yugoslav army for manoeuvres, when they had propeller planes. It's something that you can find on a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you saw these tanks on that day coming from the direction of Ambar or from Zemunik. Did you know where they came from, where they'd started moving?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you exactly where they were located. I was among them three or four days prior to that event. I was working in Sibenik. Someone from Zemunik asked a Serb who also worked with them, Zeljko Cvjetanovic. He operated an excavator. We were colleges and we dug about 60 sites in Sibenik where houses were to be constructed. I didn't want to go into details, but I was among those tanks because there is a man who has a locksmith's shop, and this man, this Serb, helped to repair something on my lorry. I wasn't an enemy of the Serbs. It's not as if we were always enemies. I then went to a shop, and that house is near the shop. And you could see all the tanks parked there from the shop. You can see the site on the map. That's where they were located. Not on the day when Skabrnja was to be attacked. They were there for 15 days or more. They had been there before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Please can I make a request. Please try to listen to the question and try to answer just the question I'm asking, because I get easily confused. Now, is Sibenik more to the west of Ambar, or where is it situated in relation to Ambar?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibenik is in the direction of Split. It's a town. It's not a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. All I want to understand is when you saw these tanks in Ambar, the first time you saw them before the attack, where did they come from? Do you know? If you don't know, just say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, they came from Oscar. It says exactly at what time they left, and it says which direction they set off in. There's an arrow indicating the direction they set off in. They left from Oscar, went through Gornji Zemunik, through the centre of Zemunik, and before Ambar some of them turned right to Polje, to reach Sveti Luka, and they encircled the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And they then moved in a generally eastern direction to come and attack Skabrnja. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was letter G that was formed. Some arrived above Razovljeva in Glavica. The army called it Glava, calls this place Glava. Others arrived from Sveti Luka. This was a carefully planned military attack. They left enough room for the civilians to withdraw if they wanted to flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll ask you once again, please try to be brief in your answers. Before the -- was it the 18th of November when -- the first attack? Before that day --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before that day, were there any tanks in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So for Skabrnja to be attacked, tanks had to come to Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came there from Oscar, from Veljane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that when you were at your brother's house before the first attack, you went onto the roof. You explained that you went on to the balcony to check, and you heard some cluster bombs being thrown; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The cluster bombs had been launched prior to that time. They weren't launched at that time. The cluster bombs were launched two days earlier. They used other devices to shell us. Multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask my question slightly differently. When the very first attack of this village took place, what had the villagers done to provoke the attack?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villagers hadn't done anything. I don't see why an attack would have been launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. That will satisfy me for purposes of that question. You were asked by Judge Hoepfel about the map. You said that you came into possession of this map two or three months ago but that you knew of its existence earlier. When did you first come to know of its existence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told about it by my neighbour Gurlica, but I didn't have the intention of using it. It wasn't necessary. He told me he had some sort of papers and this map was found among the papers that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember when he told you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, it was two or three months earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier than now when you came to testify here.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now I'm getting a little lost, because you said you came into possession of the map two or three months ago. When you say "ago," I understand that you're talking from now. But you also said you had known of its existence a little earlier. Now, you also say that you came to know of it three months ago. I'm not quite sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell you that this was an earlier map, but I said it was about three months when I found out about it. I didn't have access to that map -- or, in fact, I could have had access but I didn't insist on it. So I said three months, but I meant that I could have had access to the map but I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But the gravamen of your evidence is that you came into possession of this map two or three months ago. Is that it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, two months ago, not three, but I knew about it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You were also asked about the barracks in Knin, and you have explained that the names of these barracks, there were two, South Camp barracks and Slavko Rodic barracks. Is that correct? I think you were asked by Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the northern camp, the Sjeverni Logor, which they called Slavko Rodic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you stay -- were you detained in both of these camps?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we went to Slavko Rodic, the Slavko Rodic to spend two days there unloading ammunition. There were trailers that came from Sveti Rok, and we unloaded the ammunition there. There were some men from Lapac whom I knew who were present. As I was a haulier, I knew a lot of these people. As I was involved in transport, I knew a lot of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I'm asking you this question, because I had another question that I wanted to ask you: You testified that in Knin you were taken to the sports hall, and you call it Martic's prison, where you stayed for plus/minus three months. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That sports hall was never called Martic's prison. That must be a mistake. No one ever called it that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then let it be a mistake, because that's how the transcript explained it. In that event, then I'm not going to ask my other question. At some stage you said that while you were in detention at some stage you were asked to kiss the wall, fatherland, and the King. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We kissed it until we were exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. By the fatherland what is meant? What is meant by the fatherland? Did you know what is meant by the fatherland?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's an old thesis, an old Serbian thesis. The fatherland is what belongs to them, or what they believe belongs to them. It doesn't matter whose territory it actually is, they believed that Krajina was theirs. They would tell children that an Ustasha village had fallen when Skabrnja fell. They said that they had captured children and taken them to Benkovac in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was meant by the King?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Koenig, the German word for King. King.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But when they said you must kiss the wall, the fatherland, and the King, who did they want to kiss who is the King?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were thinking of their King who, in their eyes, was still alive; King Petar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've mentioned being kept in a small room in Knin, and you said it was something like 4 by 4 metres. I wanted to find out from you how many were you in that room?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 17 or 18 of us. That's what I say, because I never really counted, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. At some stage in Martic's prison, you said you were kept in room number 1, which was very small and could only allow a bed, and you said that one was about two and a half by two and a half metres. Oh, you did explain. You did say there were nine of you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was a small room. There were bunkbeds. There were nine of us, and there were nine beds. I meant that you could pass between the beds. You could only pass between the beds. And that's the first time I saw a bed in Knin during those 12 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You were referred, and I'm not sure whether I'm going to pronounce this word correctly, to Marticici. It sounded to me, and it looked to me when I read it here as the name "Martic" with "c-i-c-i" at the end.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If that's what I said, perhaps I said Marticevci. It would be the plural, not one person, several people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By which you meant?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the question was so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what are Marticevci? Just tell me, what are they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police or the army who operated there. Guards or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Marticevci means Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You talked of people who were in a state of delirium because they were without any alcohol and couldn't smoke. Why would people be delirious because they didn't have alcohol and they didn't smoke?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably already ill for that reason. I don't know. I know there were two such individuals. One was with me in those small houses and both of them ended up in the hall later on. And while this crisis lasted - it was for about one month- after that period of time, they calmed down to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you come to know that the cause of their delirium was lack of alcohol and lack of smoke?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easy to prove since that's what they claimed themselves. And when an addict has a crisis, that's what happens. It's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's much better, I understand you now. These people were addicts, and they told you so. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the questions by the Chamber? Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour. I simply wonder if with MFI 285, on the basis of the additional information obtained by Your Honour and Judge Hoepfel, we've reached the point where it could be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have many three brief questions in connection with questions put by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The first one refers to reservists and to your explanation, Witness, in response to Judge Nosworthy's questions. You said they were masked "but by their faces I could see they were reservists." My question is as follows: Are you trying to say that these were older men who were in the army and you concluded by their age that they were reservists? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. Between 40 and 60 years old. It was those people I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusion, you mentioned the young conscripts doing their regular military service, and now you mentioned the older people, more mature men, whom you recognised because of their age.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with these reservists, you mentioned Nada Pupovac. Was she a reservist?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She a company of her own, and she was its commander. I was told this by people from Benkovac who were ill in hospital, a butcher who had been beaten up. And this man died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, do you know whether Nada Pupovac was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was. She was from Kula -- no, not Kula, that village right next to Lisicici, but she lived and worked in Benkovac. I knew her by sight from before. I'd never had contact with her, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was she the woman you said prevented someone from cutting your throat?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a young lad that she saved. She said, I've had enough of throat slitting. So she protected that very young boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And my last question in connection with Their Honours' questions has to do with Captain Jankovic. You said you remembered him and that you're glad you remember him, and you said that he was nicknamed Lala, which would show that he came from Vojvodina, a province in Serbia. Would you say that he was a Serb or a Hungarian by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know Jankovic was a Serb. And there was a doctor in Zadar who died recently, a female doctor called Jankovic. I want to say I know people whose last name is Jankovic are usually Serbs and they're Orthodox. And in connection with these houses of worship, that woman might have been a Croat. That's what led me to believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any doubt, did I understand you correctly that you mean that Jankovic was probably a Serb, that he was Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think, what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this stage the Chamber is satisfied, unless anything else to the contrary is shown, that Exhibit 285 that was marked for identification, that's the map, can be admitted into evidence. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, Exhibit 285, which was marked for identification, is now being admitted into evidence as an exhibit. And I guess it will retain the same exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will retain the same exhibit number as Exhibit 285. Thank you very much. Mr. Brkic, thank you very much for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're most welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, in just the remaining minutes left I wonder if I could address the Chamber about a matter. I thought it might be a good time to update the Chamber on the progress that we're making in the Prosecution case, to give the Chamber a sense of where we are and when we think we might be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. The good news is that by our calculation we are well on track and we predict that we will finish within our time estimates if not earlier. You will recall that the Prosecution, in its filing of 23 November 2005, estimated as best it could that the trial would last approximately 298 hours, which is, with the trial days that we sit, is about 80 trial days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Prosecution case. Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sometimes I confuse those two. It's the Prosecution case. Yes, Your Honour. We've just completed our 37th day of evidence, so there are remaining 43 days left, which, if we sat every day that is scheduled, would take us to the 16th of June of this year. By our calculation, we will finish our evidence before then. Of course, there could -- we could mis-estimate and it could be around there, but I think we will finish earlier in June, either end of May or early June. So this is just to say that we are -- we're on track, we're within our estimates, and to give the Chamber an idea of when we think we'll finish the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Anybody wants to say anything on this? Mr. Milovancevic? Do you have any comments to make or you're quite happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting, for that update. I think it is appreciated. It is helpful to know whether we are keeping schedule or not. Is the Prosecution going to be calling a witness before we break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we're unable to fill the remaining seven minutes of the day, so we will start with our next witness on Monday. I believe we have morning court on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just check. I think you are right. Morning court in Courtroom II. This is I. We are sitting in Courtroom II, Monday morning at 9.00. Court adjourned until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
